main_point: Wikipedia and other websites are staging a global blackout to protest anti-piracy laws like SOPA and PIPA, arguing the legislation threatens the internet's future, while opponents claim the protest undermines Wikipedia's neutrality and punishes users.

statements.text: The English Wikipedia will stay offline for 24 hours to oppose new American anti-piracy laws. This choice happened because most members of the community chose a global shutdown over stopping just the US.
statements.text_short: Wikipedia plans a global 24-hour blackout to protest US anti-piracy laws.

statements.text: Wikipedia is organizing a worldwide internet shutdown to fight against strict anti-piracy legislation. This movement includes participation from large online services such as Reddit, the Boing Boing blog, and websites belonging to the Cheezburger Network.
statements.text_short: Major digital platforms are joining the global blackout to oppose anti-piracy laws.

statements.text: Proponents of the blackout argue that proposed anti-piracy laws pose an existential threat to the online encyclopedia, while critics contend that such a shutdown undermines the site's reputation for political neutrality and risks alienating the public.
statements.text_short: Blackout supporters cite an existential threat, while critics warn of lost neutrality.

statements.text: The Wikipedia co-founder told students to finish their assignments and research ahead of time. This advice was given to prevent them from being locked out of the site during a 24-hour protest targeting anti-piracy laws.
statements.text_short: Wikipedia's co-founder advised users to finish work early to avoid access issues.

statements.text: Jimmy Wales, co-founder of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, expressed hope that the planned global shutdown of the site would cause significant disruption to telecommunications infrastructure in Washington, D.C., specifically by overwhelming local phone networks with the volume of protest traffic expected during the blackout.
statements.text_short: Wales predicted the anti-piracy protest would crash Washington's phone systems.

statements.text: Jimmy Wales, co-founder of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, noted that proponents of the proposed anti-piracy legislation frame the protest movement as consisting of individuals who wish to facilitate copyright infringement, a characterization he disputes by arguing the laws themselves are poorly drafted and overly broad.
statements.text_short: Wales denied the assertion that demonstrators aim to facilitate piracy.

statements.text: Jimmy Wales, co-founder of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, argued that the proposed anti-piracy legislation is excessively broad and poorly drafted, warning that its vague provisions would negatively impact various unrelated sectors of the digital economy beyond the specific goal of stopping piracy.
statements.text_short: Wales argued the anti-piracy laws are too broad and poorly written.

statements.text: Chris Dodd, who speaks for the Motion Picture Association of America, claimed that some technology companies are organizing harmful online demonstrations. These protests hurt the companies' own customers and act as tools for corporate agendas. Dodd argued this is not a sincere attempt to fix the serious issue of online copyright infringement.
statements.text_short: The MPAA accused tech companies of staging irresponsible protests to punish users.

statements.text: The Motion Picture Association of America, which supports the proposed anti-piracy legislation, asserts that the coordinated website blackout is an irresponsible and dangerous tactic. This organization argues that the protest punishes ordinary users who rely on the internet for information, effectively turning them into corporate pawns rather than encouraging a collaborative search for solutions to the real problem of digital piracy.
statements.text_short: The Motion Picture Association of America condemns the website blackout as an irresponsible tactic that punishes users instead of solving piracy.
